title: Dental Implant Timeline: A Start-to-Finish Guide for Patients
seoTitle: Dental Implant Timeline: Start to Finish Guide
description: How long dental implants take from consultation to final crown, what adds time (infection, grafting, full-arch work) and how to plan in Santa Clarita.
excerpt: From the first CBCT scan to the final crown: the stages of implant treatment, typical timing for each, and the three things that most often stretch the schedule.
author: Dr. Neda Moezzi, DDS

keyTakeaways: Most single-tooth implants take three to nine months from extraction to crown; grafting adds three to six months.
Healing (osseointegration) typically takes 6 to 16 weeks in the lower jaw and 12 to 24 weeks in the upper jaw.
Infection and low bone volume are the two most common reasons a timeline stretches.

body:
How long will it take? That is usually the first question when a patient faces an extraction, a graft or a full reconstruction. Knowing the typical dental implant timeline helps you plan time off work, budget for the cost stages that arrive before the final crown, and understand why two clinicians might quote different schedules. For an overview of the procedure itself, start with our [dental implant service page](/services/dental-implants/).

## The stages of a typical implant timeline

From first consult to finished crown, treatment moves through a series of steps. Each one can shorten or lengthen the whole, and some add procedures such as bone grafting or a sinus lift.

- **Consult, imaging and planning.** 3D CBCT scan, digital intraoral scans and a medical review.
- **Preparatory care.** Extractions, gum treatment or socket preservation grafting when needed.
- **Implant placement.** Immediate, early or delayed, depending on infection and bone.
- **Healing and osseointegration.** The implant fuses with bone over weeks to months.
- **Abutment and restoration.** A healing or custom abutment, then a provisional and finally the definitive crown, bridge or denture.
- **Maintenance.** Regular hygiene visits and periodic checks of the prosthesis.

## Timeline table: start to finish

| Stage | Typical timing | What it means for you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consult and imaging | 1 to 2 visits over 1 to 3 weeks | Initial plan, cost estimate, CBCT scan and medical clearance if needed |
| Extraction, with or without socket graft | Immediate to 2 weeks | Socket preservation reduces the chance of major grafting later |
| Implant placement | Same day to 16 weeks after extraction, depending on infection and bone | Immediate placement saves time but is not possible when infection is present |
| Osseointegration (healing) | 6 to 16 weeks in the lower jaw; 12 to 24 weeks in the upper jaw | Bone quality and grafting lengthen this phase |
| Restoration (abutment and crown) | 2 to 6 visits over 2 to 8 weeks | Final crown or fixed prosthesis is delivered once integration is stable |

## Why timings vary

Three factors most often change the schedule: existing infection, bone volume and quality, and the restorative plan. Infection forces a delay so the body can clear bacteria before a titanium or zirconia implant is placed. Low bone height or width usually means grafting. Complex prosthetics such as full-arch fixed bridges add surgical and laboratory stages.

Patients describing their own cases often mention the same frustrations: different clinicians quoting different timelines, waiting for infection to clear, and graft healing that took longer than expected. Some also notice small gritty particles after a socket graft; this is a known sensation as particulate graft material settles and integrates. All of it points to the same conclusion: your timeline should be individualized and written down.

## Immediate, early or delayed placement

- **Immediate placement.** The implant goes in at the extraction visit. Shortest overall timeline. Best when the socket is free of infection and the implant can be made stable on the day.
- **Early placement.** The implant is placed after the soft tissue heals but before bone remodeling is complete, commonly 6 to 12 weeks after extraction.
- **Delayed placement.** The implant is placed after full healing, sometimes after grafting, often 4 months or more after extraction.

Which approach fits depends on local bone, infection status and the prosthetic goal. Peer-reviewed reviews report survival rates near 90 to 95 percent at five years when cases are well selected and maintained; the American Dental Association and systematic reviews on PubMed are good places to review those figures with your clinician.

## How bone grafting changes the timeline and cost

Grafting adds predictable healing time. A particulate socket preservation graft commonly needs three to four months to mature before an implant is placed. Larger block grafts or sinus lifts often need four to six months or more. These steps add cost and visits but preserve options and improve long-term stability. For more detail, see our [bone grafting healing timeline](/bone-grafting-healing-timeline/) and our overview of [dental implant costs](/dental-implants-cost/).

## Pain and recovery: what most patients experience

Discomfort is usually greatest in the first 48 to 72 hours and then eases. Most patients manage with short courses of over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medication and, occasionally, a prescription. Swelling peaks around 48 hours and settles within a week. Expect two to seven days of light activity after surgery and three to six months of follow-up through the healing phase. Some surgeons place provisional crowns at about two months in low-risk lower-jaw cases; others wait three to six months or longer in the upper jaw because the bone is less dense.

## Time and likely cost by treatment pathway

The cost ranges below are typical U.S. figures, not our fees.

| Pathway | Usual total time | Typical per-tooth cost range (U.S.) | When it fits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate implant with provisional crown | 3 to 4 months | $3,000 to $6,000 | Strong bone, no infection, high esthetic need |
| Delayed implant after socket graft | 5 to 8 months | $4,000 to $7,500 | Lost bone volume or infection that required grafting |
| Full-arch staged All-on-X | 4 to 12 months including provisional phases | $15,000 to $30,000 per arch | Multiple failing teeth or a toothless arch |

## Scheduling in Santa Clarita

Wait times for specialist appointments vary, and academic clinics can have long scheduling windows that add months on their own. Booking imaging and your consultation early is the simplest way to keep the total time down. At Valencia Dentistry, Dr. Neda Moezzi handles planning, guided implant surgery and the restoration in one office, so you see a complete timeline and staged cost estimate up front. For what happens at each visit, see [how long dental implants take](/how-long-do-dental-implants-take/).

## Complications that extend the timeline

Three issues most often add time: persistent infection, insufficient bone that needs a larger graft, and mechanical problems with the prosthesis that require a remake. Infection is cleared first, which may mean weeks of antibiotics or debridement. Staged grafts add several months before the final restoration. A written schedule and honest communication reduce surprises.

## Questions to ask before you commit

- Who will place the implant and who will make the restoration?
- What is the proposed timing for each stage, and what could realistically add time?
- If grafting is needed, what material will be used and how long should it heal?
- How are complications handled, and what follow-up is included in the price?
- Can I see before-and-after photos of similar cases?

## Next steps

Infection and low bone are the two main reasons implant timelines stretch. Immediate placement suits selected cases only, and staged grafting adds months but tends to improve the result. For a personalized timeline that lists every visit, healing window and cost stage, schedule a CBCT-based consultation with Dr. Moezzi in Valencia. Call (661) 254-5200.

faq.q: How long does the whole dental implant timeline take from extraction to crown?
faq.a: Most single-tooth cases without major grafting take three to nine months from extraction to crown. Socket preservation or grafting adds three to six months. Full-arch reconstructions and complex grafts can run six to twelve months or longer. Ask for a staged timeline specific to your anatomy.

faq.q: Can I get an implant on the same day as extraction?
faq.a: Sometimes. Immediate placement is possible when there is no infection and the socket allows good initial stability. It shortens the calendar but is not always the safest route; with infection or poor bone, early or delayed placement protects the long-term result.

faq.q: How long after implant placement will I get the permanent crown?
faq.a: Permanent crowns are typically placed after osseointegration, commonly six to sixteen weeks in the lower jaw and twelve to twenty-four weeks in the upper jaw. Some clinicians fit a provisional crown earlier for appearance but wait for confirmed integration before the final crown.

faq.q: How long does bone graft healing take before an implant can be placed?
faq.a: Socket preservation grafts often need three to four months. Larger grafts such as vertical augmentation or sinus lifts commonly need four to six months. Exact timing depends on graft type, your health and the site.

faq.q: What are signs that my implant needs more time to heal?
faq.a: Pain that increases after the first post-operative week, persistent swelling, a loose healing cap or bone loss on X-ray suggest healing is not on track. Contact your provider promptly if new symptoms appear.

faq.q: Will a history of infection delay my implant timeline?
faq.a: Yes. Active infection at the extraction site is the most frequent reason clinicians delay placement. The area must be cleaned out and often grafted before the implant goes in, which protects integration and lowers the risk of early failure.
